intro: The most common reason Bonnyrigg homeowners pick up the phone about leak detection is a water bill that's crept up for no obvious reason, or a damp patch on a wall or ceiling that won't dry out. Leaks aren't always dramatic — a slow drip behind a wall or under a floor can go unnoticed for months, causing serious damage to plasterwork, joinery, and even structural timbers before you realise what's happening. Getting a plumber in quickly to locate and repair the source properly — rather than just patching over visible damp — is almost always cheaper than dealing with the secondary damage later.
localContext: Bonnyrigg's housing stock creates some fairly predictable leak hotspots. The older stone-built properties and period cottages that are common across the town were built with lead or iron pipework in many cases, and those materials degrade over time — particularly around joints and where pipes pass through solid walls. Even where original pipework has been replaced, the replumbing was often done in phases over decades, leaving a mix of materials that can react poorly with each other and cause pinhole corrosion. The modern estates on the edges of Bonnyrigg are generally better insulated, but they bring their own issues: plastic push-fit joints that can work loose, and concealed pipework in floor voids that's difficult to access without specialist equipment. Bonnyrigg sits in a moderately hard water area, which means limescale build-up is a factor — particularly on boiler connections, shower valves, and any older copper pipework, where scale can cause micro-cracks and weeping joints over time.
serviceDetail: When you call a plumber for leak detection in Bonnyrigg, the first step is a thorough visual inspection — checking under sinks, around the boiler, at radiator valves, and any accessible pipework. If the source isn't immediately obvious, a good tradesperson will move on to more targeted methods. Acoustic listening equipment is commonly used to detect the sound of water escaping through a pipe, even through solid walls or floors. Thermal imaging cameras are another useful tool, showing temperature differences in walls or ceilings caused by cool water tracking through a structure. For underground supply pipes or leaks between the meter and the property, tracer gas detection — where a harmless gas is introduced into the pipe and detected at the surface — is often the most accurate method. Once the source is confirmed, the plumber will discuss repair options with you before starting work. Minor repairs such as replacing a joint, reseating a valve, or fitting a new section of pipe are typically straightforward. More involved repairs — cutting into tiled areas, lifting floorboards, or re-routing a run of pipework — take longer and cost more, but a good tradesperson will give you a clear quote before they start. You should always receive confirmation of the repair and a check to make sure pressure is restored before they leave.
pricing: In Bonnyrigg, you can expect to pay roughly £80–£150 for a callout and initial leak detection, depending on whether specialist equipment is needed. Simple repairs — replacing a joint, tightening a compression fitting, or swapping out a valve — typically fall in the £100–£200 range including labour and parts. More complex jobs, such as tracing and repairing a concealed pipe leak behind tiling or under a concrete floor, can run from £250 to £500 or more, particularly if remedial work like replastering or retiling is needed afterwards. Emergency callouts outside normal hours will carry a premium on top of these figures.
whyLocal: A plumber who works regularly in Bonnyrigg will have a good working knowledge of the town's housing stock — they'll know the quirks of the older stone-built terraces, be familiar with the pipe layouts common in period cottages around the town centre, and understand the typical installation standards on the newer estates. That local familiarity genuinely speeds up a job. They're also more likely to be available quickly, won't be charging travel time from Edinburgh, and their reputation is built locally — which tends to keep standards high. Word travels fast in a town of Bonnyrigg's size.

faqs.q: My water meter is turning when everything is switched off — does that definitely mean I have a leak?
faqs.a: Almost certainly yes. The standard test is to note your meter reading, avoid using any water for an hour, then check again. If the dial has moved, water is escaping somewhere. In Bonnyrigg's older properties, the supply pipe between the street meter and the house is a common culprit — it's worth having this checked first as it's the section most likely to have deteriorated.

faqs.q: How much damage can a slow leak really cause if I leave it a few weeks?
faqs.a: Quite a lot, unfortunately. In stone-built Bonnyrigg properties, water tracks through walls quickly and can saturate lime plaster, cause timber lintels to rot, and promote mould growth behind finishes.

faqs.q: Will the plumber need to cut into my walls or lift floors to find the leak?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Modern acoustic and thermal imaging equipment can often pinpoint a leak without any destructive investigation. If access is required, a good tradesperson will keep it to a minimum and explain clearly what's needed before starting. In Bonnyrigg's older properties with solid stone walls, non-invasive detection equipment is particularly valuable as cutting into stone is a significant job.

faqs.q: Is limescale likely to be causing my leaking pipes in Bonnyrigg?
faqs.a: It can be a contributing factor. Bonnyrigg's moderately hard water causes gradual limescale deposits inside pipework, which can put stress on older copper joints and cause weeping at fittings over time. It also affects shower valves and boiler connections. A plumber can advise whether a scale inhibitor or water softener would help reduce the risk of repeat issues in your property.
